title: The World of AI: Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations page
answer: This is a The World of AI ecosystem page cataloguing four individually verified nonprofits and open source foundations with sourced classification notes. Its most useful point is that only one entry, LMSYS, is directly AI central because it stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform for benchmarking model quality. sections.body: The World of AI publishes this ecosystem page, titled Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations. It is a catalogue of four individually verified organisations, each with a sourced classification note, and it sits within a larger site covering AI laws, lawsuits, a glossary, tools, companies, research, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests. The page says every page is rebuilt daily from primary sources and carries the date it was last verified. The citation gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-29. The page also promotes books by Stephen R. Jordan and SRJ Consulting services.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page lists four organisations: two nonprofits and two open source foundations with roles that touch AI tooling and evaluation, but none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS is the most directly AI central entry. It stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the broader AI community uses to benchmark model quality. The page says this open evaluation infrastructure matters because model comparison depends on it and sits outside the labs' commercial incentives. Khan Academy is an end user of AI capability in education, not a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that AI generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, but their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. Each classification was made one at a time against a document the organisation published about itself. Every entry carries the source that decided it and the date that source was last read. Nothing was assigned by keyword, by a model, or by inheritance from a parent company, because a classification that keeps no evidence cannot be audited and a wrong one survives quietly. It does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies setting grid or data center specifications, or open model foundations that release weights for public use. The list is small, four entries, and the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page gives one number: four individually verified organisations, described as two nonprofits and two open source foundations. It names LMSYS, Khan Academy, Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation. It defines LMSYS as the most directly AI central entry and Chatbot Arena as a shared evaluation platform. It states none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. It also states the notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status only, not funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in nonprofits can use this page as a small, sourced starting point for identifying nonprofit and open source organisations whose roles touch AI tooling and evaluation. It is most useful for seeing how one AI central nonprofit, LMSYS, supports shared model evaluation through Chatbot Arena, and for separating that from nonprofits that mainly use AI, such as Khan Academy, or steward creative software that AI content intersects with, such as Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation. It also shows the catalogue does not explain nonprofit influence on compute, power or open model release.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The page is partial and small. It covers only four entries and says the notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access or governance detail. It does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies setting grid or data center specifications, or open model foundations that release weights for public use. It is also commercial in part, promoting books by Stephen R. Jordan and SRJ Consulting services, including audits and a novel. The page says it is rebuilt daily and carries verification dates, but the supplied text does not give individual last read dates for the four entries.
